Can religion bridge ethnic divides? How pastors in the DRC promote collective action where chiefs cannot: Guest post by Gabriel Granato

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 13, 2026

This is the seventh in this year’s job market series.
Where governments lack resources for basic infrastructure, communities rely on informal arrangements to organize contributions of labor, money, and materials to maintain public goods. Yet, sustaining individual contributions can be challenging in ethnically diverse settings, as such divisions may create obstacles to enforcing social sanctions that prevent residents from free-riding on neighbors’ contributions. In principle, local leaders could help solve this enforcement problem. But chiefs, the authorities best placed to do so, also have their influence constrained by ethnicity. Who, then, can bridge ethnic divides?
Religious leaders are natural candidates. In large parts of the developing world, they play important roles—from conflict resolution to job training to service provision—and are central to many communities’ livelihoods. Importantly, they differ from chiefs in two crucial ways. Their scope of authority extends beyond the ethnic group, and research has documented a correlation between moralizing religions and cooperation. Second, rather than relying on social sanctions, religious leaders can appeal to internal religious motives (e.g., fear of divine judgment) that do not require an audience of peers.
Our paper tests whether this intuition holds: can religious leaders sustain cooperation where ethnic divisions limit chiefs’ influence? Would a shared faith be enough to induce costly contributions across ethnic lines? And would chiefs really fail to enforce contributions from residents of other origins? We cannot answer these questions by comparing existing communities: apparently effective leaders might simply have more cooperative residents.
Randomizing collective action in Kananga
To test whether religious leaders can sustain cooperation where ethnic divisions limit chiefs’ influence, we partnered with the city administration of Kananga, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), during a campaign to encourage participation in salongo—a longstanding community-labor institution in which residents repair roads, remove waste, and protect neighborhoods from erosion (Figure 1, top).
As part of the campaign, the administration introduced a contribution-tracking system and organized volunteer teams for public maintenance over several weeks. We helped implement the program and randomly assigned teams to include a chief, a pastor, or no leader. We also varied whether teams assembled residents who shared the chief’s ethno-territorial origin (homogeneous) or came from different origins (mixed). The experiment covered 1,040 participants across 336 teams.
Figure 1. Community work and meetings

 
 
Why would Kananga leaders differ in their ability to engage residents? In the DRC, chiefs coordinate salongo through established authority rooted in an ethnically organized political system. They should be able to reach coethnics but may struggle across origins. Kananga’s independent “born-again” churches are part of a worldwide Pentecostal revival. These widespread neighborhood institutions often cross ethnic divides, and their local pastors frame community service as a moral obligation.
Nevertheless, chiefs remain local authorities even for residents who do not share their origins, while volunteers on campaign teams may belong to different denominations, sharing only a broad Christian faith. Will ethnic differences really limit chiefs’ influence? Will a broad religious connection be enough for pastors to sustain cooperation?
Ethnic diversity changed who could organize collective action
Our first finding is that ethnic cohesion alone did not improve participation. In teams without a leader, residents participated in public works on roughly half the days they could, averaging around 13 hours of work per week per volunteer, with similar participation across homogeneous and mixed teams. A leader’s presence changed this pattern. Chiefs increased participation by 6 percentage points in homogeneous teams but had little effect in mixed teams. Pastors produced the opposite pattern: participation rose by 5.8 percentage points in mixed teams, with no detectable effect in homogeneous teams. When compared to volunteers’ contributions in teams without a leader, these gains amount to roughly an extra hour per week (Figure 2, top panel).
Figure 2. Leader effects

 
 
Why pastors fail in homogeneous teams?
But if religion reaches across ethnic boundaries, why would pastors have less influence within them? Could the same ethnic ties that enable chiefs also limit pastors? Our findings suggest that chiefs’ influence is greater in homogeneous teams where residents strongly identify with their ethnicity, and that coethnics also respond to chiefs in mixed teams. Ethnic ties appear to matter partly because they predict more consequential relationships with the chief, giving residents stronger social incentives to contribute.
For pastors, ethnic attachment matters differently. In homogeneous teams, their influence is positive where ethnic attachment is weak and negative where it is strong, suggesting that religious appeals may displace stronger ethnic obligations. In mixed groups, where such attachments may reinforce divisions rather than provide a shared reason for cooperation, the pattern reverses. Pastors become more effective as residents identify more strongly with their respective ethnicities, suggesting that religious appeals matter most when they provide a common basis for cooperation where ethnic attachments divide the group.
Could these patterns simply reflect differences in religious commitment? We find little evidence that residents with stronger ethnic attachment are less religious. Religiosity, nevertheless, matters for how residents respond to pastors: their effects are concentrated among those who treat religion as a guiding principle. In sum, our evidence points to an account where team ethnic cohesion makes cooperation primarily a socially enforced ethnic obligation and constrains a religious framing of participation.
How leaders enforce contributions?
Do residents contribute because they expect others to observe and judge their behavior, or because they feel an obligation even when others are not watching? As part of the program, teams met to review their contributions and coordinate future participation. Residents could contribute at different times and worksites, so teammates otherwise had incomplete knowledge of one another’s efforts. Thus, we cross-randomized whether these meetings disclosed each member’s participation or only the team’s total contribution to distinguish whether pastors and chiefs enforced participation through different channels (Figure 2, bottom).
Chiefs’ positive effects in homogeneous teams were concentrated where individual participation was disclosed—where the group fell within their authority, and they could judge individual behavior. This reinforces an interpretation based on social enforcement. Pastors produced a different pattern: they increased participation in mixed teams without individual disclosure, but their estimated effect fell toward zero when contributions became public. This is contrary to what we would expect if pastors also relied on social pressure to encourage participation (Figure 2, bottom panel).
These effects, combined with other triangulating evidence, are consistent with an account in which chiefs and pastors influence participants through fundamentally different mechanisms: chiefs rely on external incentives enforced through social accountability, while pastors appeal to internalized religious obligations.
Policy Implications
Our campaign shows that community contributions can be a major source of local fiscal capacity. Across 28 neighborhoods covering an estimated 14% of city households, residents supplied 70,250 hours across an estimated 832 worksites. Valuing labor at a local public-works wage, contributions including cash and materials totaled roughly $28,000—nearly a third of provincial 2025 property-tax receipts. Matching leaders and accountability to communities could yield another 75 worksites’ worth of labor.
In Kananga, fragmentation was not a barrier to collective action; it changed which leaders could govern cooperation. For policy in diverse cities, these findings point to the value of implementation partners whose influence crosses ethnic boundaries. Their capacity to mobilize mixed constituencies can help sustain cooperation where authority rooted in a single community falls short. In future work, I hope to study how local leaders may serve other capacity building efforts and facilitate governance in weak states.
Gabriel Granato is a PhD student at the University of California, Berkeley.
